passages.original: eloquentia clarus, poemate inter sui temporis poetas praecipuus, vini, cibi, Veneriae avidus, vestitu cultus, nec quicquam defuit quod illum populo non commendabilem redderet, amabilis etiam senatui fuit. passages.english: Distinguished for eloquence, foremost in poetry among the poets of his time, greedy for wine, food and love-making, elegant in dress, there was nothing lacking that might fail to make him agreeable to the people, and he was also loved by the senate. This is what we have found out about the life of each of them. Finally, some have thought that, just as Sallust compares Cato and Caesar, so these two should also be compared, so that [they would call] the one stern, the other merciful, the former good, the latter steadfast, the former bestowing nothing, the latter abun-
passages.notes: The passage breaks off mid-word: 'arflu-' is evidently a scanning error for 'adflu-' / 'afflu-' (affluentem, 'abundant [in all things]'), with the rest of the word and sentence not supplied. 'Veneriae' is presumably for 'Veneris' or 'rei Veneriae' (sexual pleasure). The double negative 'nec quicquam defuit quod illum populo non commendabilem redderet' is rendered literally; the sense is that he had every quality that endeared him to the people. The comparison echoes Sallust, Catiline 54.
